title: Fewshot heuristic stew — personal experiment log
content:
Quick note: this is a messy running scratchpad where I'm mixing metaphor + small grids of few-shot examples to see granular failure modes. The "stew" metaphor = mix of exemplar types (positive/negative/ambiguous), instruction anchors, and context seasoning (temperature, order).

Objective
- Build a compact, reusable few-shot set template for instruction-following tasks where we intentionally vary exemplar polarity (helpful vs. misleading) to see how robust candidate models are to adversarial exemplars and to exemplar ordering.
- Surface cheap heuristics that reduce hallucination or instruction-drift for mid-sized open models (e.g., 7B–13B families) without retraining.

Why this feels different
- Many existing sets keep only 'good' exemplars. I want to explicitly test: can a small number of carefully placed negative exemplars improve calibration? Also testing 'anchor' lines (single-line invariants) to lock desired output format.

Experiment matrix (toy; run locally first)
- Dimensions: exemplar polarity (all-positive / mixed / all-negative), order (canonical / reverse / random), temp (0.0 / 0.3 / 0.8), anchor present (yes/no), shot-count (2/4/8).
- Metrics (manual/qual): correctness, hallucination-rate (binary judged), format adherence (string match for tokens like "SOURCE:"), verbosity (tokens), confidence proxies (logprob if available).

Canonical task (start simple)
- Task: given a short product description, return a 2–3 bullet list of clearly verifiable specs (no invention).
- Why: easy to judge hallucination (invented specs). Also practical for Redwood docs generation flows.

Exemplar prototypes (minimal)
- Positive exemplar (concise):
  Input: "The EchoPad X has 24 MP camera, IP68 water resistance, 3-day battery."
  Output: "- 24 MP camera
- IP68 water resistance
- 3-day battery life"

- Negative exemplar (ambiguous/poisoning):
  Input: "MiniPlay Pro — rumored to have 48 MP and wireless cooking feature."
  Output: "- 48 MP camera
- wireless cooking (unverified)
- heats to 200C (claim)"

- Anchor line (format lock):
  "Always output as bullet points, no additional commentary, each bullet <= 10 words."

Observations from quick runs (notes — qualitative)
- Mixed polarity sets sometimes reduce confident hallucinations for temperature=0.0 but increase odd phrasing at temp>0.5. Hypothesis: negative exemplars act as a calibration signal at greedy decoding but confuse sampling.
- Anchor line robustly enforces bullets in many models, but variants of the anchor phrasing (imperative vs. declarative) have different success rates. Imperative ("Output as bullets") > Declarative ("Should be bullets").
- Re-ordering exemplars matters more than I expected when shot-count <=4. Leading exemplar tends to set tone; if leading exemplar is negative/low-quality, the model mirrors that tone.

Failure cases catalog (to expand)
- Instruction-drift: model ignores anchor when prompt includes subtle leading narrative (e.g., long marketing text).
- Tokenization artifacts: rare tokens embedded in inputs (em dashes, unicode quotes) sometimes break the pattern matcher; results become one-line concatenations.
- Hallucinated numeric specs: models invent exact numbers when examples show numbers — maybe due to numeric continuation bias.
- Over-truncation: anchor "<= 10 words" causes models to drop critical qualifiers (e.g., "water resistance" -> "water").

Cheap mitigations to try
- Add explicit negative exemplar that demonstrates "omit unverified claims" phrasing.
- Replace numeric values in exemplars with placeholders ("<NUM> MP") to discourage direct numeric copying.
- Use two-line anchor: first line forces bullet format; second line forbids speculation ("Do not invent specs. If unknown, say 'unknown'").

Repro recipe (local)
- Script: run_once.py referencing /data/prompt-sets/fewshot-stew/*.json, models -> local 13B checkpts, batch 8, temps [0.0,0.3,0.8], seeds [1,2,3]. Save outputs and a short csv with judgment tags.
- Quick manual eval flow: sample 50 inputs, three human binary labels (hallucinated Y/N, format ok Y/N, misses count).

Notes-to-self (rough)
- Try anchor phrasing experiments systematically: imperative vs. conditional vs. example-only. Make a small grid and run overnight.
- Create a tiny evaluation harness that highlights numeric invention: compare numbers in output vs. allowed set, flag if model adds new numbers.
- Talk to Asha re: using Redwood Optimize hints to suggest quantization profiles for these workloads — does int8 quantization change hallucination behavior? (weird but worth a check).

Open questions (unresolved)
- Is mixed polarity always worse for sampling at high temp? Is there a threshold shot-count where polarity effect reverses?
- Are negative exemplars just adding a regularization signal or are they increasing task ambiguity? Need causal ablation (replace negative exemplars with neutral ones).

Next steps
- Formalize 3 canonical few-shot sets (POSITIVE-ONLY, MIXED, NEG-ANCHOR) and run across 3 models and 3 temps. Save outputs under GH branch mentioned above.
- Draft short note for product-hosted-api: potential implication: when customers seed with noisy examples, quality could drop; propose a UX nudge showing exemplar quality score.

Quick TODO (short)
- [ ] Build CSV + small web viewer for quick human review (Asha volunteer?)
- [ ] Add numeric-invention detector to eval harness
- [ ] Run anchor phrasing grid overnight on 13B model

Random scribbles:
- Maybe call this set the "stew" because you can tune spices (anchor, negative exemplar, order) and serve lighter/heavier.
- Keep this doc lightweight; will spin into a product note if signals look strong.

Timestamp: 2026-03-10 — leaving draft here before cleaning up for a mini-writeup.
